claims.text: As-processed HfNbTiVAl10 has a well-characterized hierarchical heterostructure.
The hierarchical heterostructure in HfNbTiVAl10 includes phase boundaries and intragranular nanoprecipitates.

Combining quantitative microstructural descriptors, first-principles-derived parameters, and machine-learning regression will predict the mechanical properties of HfNbTiVAl10 faster and more accurately than established full-scale simulations.
The proposed framework will use the spatial distribution and size of heterostructural features as model inputs.
Misfit volumes, elastic constants, and stacking-fault-related energies are relevant first-principles inputs to strengthening and ductility models.
Nano- and mesoscale heterostructural features govern local mechanical responses and dislocation interactions in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates can enhance dislocation accumulation and storage.
Enhanced dislocation storage associated with a hierarchical architecture can increase strain hardening and ductility.
Explicit microstructural parameters will allow the model to capture solid-solution and heterostructure-induced strengthening in HfNbTiVAl10.
The modeled strengthening mechanisms govern elastic behavior, plastic behavior, and fracture behavior.
Physics-informed machine learning will accelerate prediction by bypassing computationally expensive full-scale DFT or atomistic simulations.
The proposed model will reduce predictive error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional simulations.
The proposed model will reduce computation time by a factor of 5–10 relative to conventional simulations.

Direct first-principles evaluation of alloy yield strength and fracture is generally beyond available DFT implementations, and first-principles simulations of disordered mult principal-element alloys remain challenging.
Established DFT and continuum simulations do not explicitly account for the hierarchical heterostructure details of HfNbTiVAl10.
The microstructure remains unchanged during room-temperature testing at typical loading rates.
The approach may fail if its descriptors omit important inelastic interactions or if phase transformations or thermal aging alter the heterostructure during testing.
Predictive gains depend on the representativeness of the descriptors and the quality of the training data.

The hypothesis is predeclared as falsified if independent tests show less than about a 20% reduction in predictive error or less than a fivefold reduction in simulation time relative to established methods.
